samples.prompt: Write a reflective narrative about revisiting a memory from your youth involving an unfinished or newly constructed building. Describe your philosophical impressions of the empty structure at the time and include a specific incident or action you took during your visit.
samples.generated: I went back to the town where I spent my early days and saw the old house again. I had been there before; but this time it was different. I did not go in the house, but outside it, to see the house that was going up. It was a very good piece of work, so far as I could judge. The men were all busy; and they were busy with the new building, which stood on the old building. They seemed to think that they ought to be doing something in the way of making the old house get out of the way. But the old house refused, and stood up like a man of the first rank. It looked as though it would last as long as the earth lasted.

Use an extended metaphor involving a common object to illustrate the difference between these approaches.
samples.generated: The two modes of reasoning I am to compare are those that begin with first principles, and those that start with immediate observations, and work backward; the one being like a man who takes his measures from his first principles, the other like a man who measures from the last thing he came by, which is as far from the first as he went from it before. The man that works from first principles has his eye on the first idea that occurred to him, and he will see the next idea as clearly as he saw the first, and so on; but the man that works backwards, like a man who goes home from a tavern without knowing how he got there, has no idea of going back; and though he may see his way, like a good steward, when he comes to do his work, yet if he be asked what was the business of his master, he can tell him nothing.

samples.prompt: Write a personal essay that revisits a place from your past, comparing how it appears now with your memories of it from years ago.
samples.generated:
It was a very long time before I could even begin to think of this town as a city, but at last I did. Then I came back again. Now I have come back to the city, and I can see the old streets again, with all their familiar sights and sounds, and there is something in the atmosphere which makes me feel like a boy.
The town is very much as it used to be, only more so. It is bigger, and there are many more stores, but still they are the same kind of stores: the same stores as were here then, but bigger and better. There are more shops for men’s wear than there used to be, and more of everything. But if you take out the new shops and the new buildings and the new people and the new cars and the new telephones, the old town is just the same as ever.
I have seen this place in a way which has always been my own. I saw it when I first went away; I saw it again when I went back to it, and I see it now. It is like a dream to me, which is true because I dreamed it. When I was young it seemed to me a town that had no other business but mine. It was my town, and I was its master. I was the lord of it, and I ruled it. I was its head and heart, and it was my soul.
Now the town is a great city, and my own town, the one I was born in, the one where I spent my childhood, the one I knew best, is the town of my youth. But it is still the same town that was always the same to me.

that he paid a call at his own house. My own absent-mindedness is
extreme, and my philosophy, of course, is the marvel of men and angels.
But I never quite managed to be so absent-minded as that. Some yards at

constantly walked into another man's house, thinking it was my own
house; my visits became almost monotonous. But walking into my own house
